items.title: Zelda Williams urges fans to stop creating AI videos of late father Robin Williams, calling them disrespectful and unconvincing [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Robin Williams' Daughter to Fans Creating AI Videos: 'Have Some Shame'
items.summary:
Zelda Williams, daughter of the late actor Robin Williams, has publicly condemned fans who create and share AI-generated videos featuring her father's likeness. She described a circulating AI video as unconvincing and robotic, urging creators to respect her father's legacy and stop using his image in such content.

Zelda has previously expressed her discomfort with AI recreations of her father and recently revived his Instagram account with her siblings to combat misuse of his voice and likeness. She emphasized that her father should not be treated as a puppet after his death and called for decency from fans and content creators.

items.title: SpaceXAI launches Grok 4.7, a faster, more capable AI model for coding and knowledge work with improved safety and lower cost [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Grok 4.7
items.summary:
SpaceXAI has released Grok 4.7, its most advanced AI model designed for coding and professional knowledge tasks. The model offers twice the speed and half the price of comparable models, with enhanced ability to handle complex, long-duration tasks and improved self-verification. It also features stronger safeguards against misuse, particularly in cybersecurity and biosafety contexts.

Grok 4.7 builds on a larger base model and extended reinforcement learning, improving performance on benchmarks involving professional work such as legal and financial analysis. It incorporates a new safeguard stack that reduces risky prompt acceptance while maintaining utility for legitimate security tasks. The model is available now via Cursor, Grok Build, API, and third-party platforms, with pricing starting at $2 per million input tokens and $6 per million output tokens.

items.title: Linear reworks CI pipeline to reduce bottlenecks caused by faster AI-assisted coding, cutting pull request wait times and runner usage despite quadrupled test suites [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: AI coding has made CI a bottleneck, so we reworked ours to keep up
items.summary:
Linear identified continuous integration (CI) as a bottleneck due to accelerated AI-assisted coding and undertook a comprehensive overhaul to improve performance. The company upgraded infrastructure, optimized job execution, reduced redundant setup, and enhanced test efficiency, resulting in a reduction of pull request wait times from over six minutes to just over five and halving runner time per test despite a near quadrupling of test suites.

Key improvements included moving workloads off GitHub Actions to faster third-party runners, switching to a native TypeScript compiler to cut type checking times, rewriting lint rules to avoid type checking dependencies, and optimizing job gating by limiting fetch depth and improving checkout resilience. These changes collectively reduced CI costs and improved developer feedback speed, with many optimizations applicable beyond Linear's primarily TypeScript codebase.

items.title: Tim Dettmers' lab launches Open Source Week to demonstrate frontier AI research on accessible hardware with open ecosystems [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Frontier AI on Your Own Hardware
items.summary:
Tim Dettmers' lab is promoting a renaissance in academic AI research by releasing an open-source ecosystem designed to enable frontier autonomous research on modest hardware like a few GPUs or even a MacBook. The initiative, called Open Source Week, focuses on building interconnected AI components that improve each other, emphasizing accessibility by reducing both hardware and expertise requirements.

The lab's approach includes an agent harness that automates optimization tasks over extended periods without user intervention, achieving efficient inference performance such as quantized models running at high speed with low memory usage. This work challenges the notion that cutting-edge AI research requires massive GPU resources and aims to empower university labs and individual researchers to contribute significantly to AI advancements.

items.title: Institute for Advanced Study launches independent Advisory Group on Mathematics and Artificial Intelligence to guide AI companies on mathematical research interactions [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: The Advisory Group on Mathematics and Artificial Intelligence
items.summary:
The Institute for Advanced Study in Princeton has established the Advisory Group on Mathematics and Artificial Intelligence to advise AI companies on their engagement with mathematical research and the mathematical community. The group, composed of prominent mathematicians, aims to ensure responsible presentation and release of AI-generated mathematical results while maintaining independence from AI companies.

Formed after OpenAI approached some members about creating an external advisory board, the group operates without accepting payment and publishes recommendations publicly. Its current focus is advising OpenAI on coordinating the release of significant mathematical findings produced by its internal AI model, and it invites input from the broader mathematical community to inform its guidance.

items.title: Kev launches small Jev-like decision models based on Qwen3.5 with pretrained weights and training code [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Kev: Tiny Jev-like family of decision models built on top of Qwen3.5
items.summary:
Kev is a family of compact decision models built on Qwen3.5, inspired by Jev's architecture, allowing users to train and run models locally or use pretrained weights. The models support yes/no, multiple-choice, and rating questions in a single request and run efficiently on CUDA and Apple Silicon hardware. Kev offers models of 0.8B, 4B, and 9B parameters, with APIs compatible with TypeSafe's System One SDK and a web playground for testing inputs and option order effects.

Users can start Kev locally with Python 3.12+ and uv, sending queries that return probabilistic answers for multiple question types, useful for tasks like customer support ticket classification. The project includes training code, evaluation data, and demos such as a chess game where Kev rates positions and suggests moves. Kev-4B is recommended for general use, with larger models available for higher accuracy and calibration needs.

items.title: Developer releases autonomous accounting tool that uses AI to process receipts, invoices, and bank statements into reconciled ledgers and audit binders [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: I built an autonomous accounting tool to let AI do my taxes
items.summary:
A developer created an autonomous accounting tool that leverages a vision large language model (LLM) to read financial documents and automate tax-related bookkeeping. The tool processes receipts, invoices, and bank statements into structured data, performs multi-pass reconciliation, categorizes expenses, and generates reports including tax summaries and audit binders, all running locally without sending data to external servers.

The system flags uncertain matches for user review instead of guessing, supports multiple currencies with strict rules, and emphasizes data privacy by operating entirely on the user's machine. It integrates with PostgreSQL and requires Python, Node.js, and an OpenAI-compatible vision endpoint, but does not host any AI models itself. The project aims to streamline tax preparation while maintaining accuracy and security.

items.summary:

The tool supports recursive delegation, durable state persistence, and interruption recovery to improve reliability in AI workflows.

The system allows managers to delegate tasks, track progress through checkpoints, and integrate results without continuous polling, enabling flexible workflows that can run sequentially or in parallel. It includes a visual console for designing and operating teams, supports multiple AI providers like Codex and Claude, and ensures that task ownership and results remain transparent and recoverable even after interruptions.

This approach aims to reduce the complexity of coordinating multiple AI agents by providing a stable runtime contract for responsibility and accountability, preserving workflow history, and enabling reusable team structures that adapt dynamically to different tasks and evidence.

items.summary:
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told CNBC that artificial intelligence developers need to take responsibility for their actions rather than relying on a federal liability shield, emphasizing that humans, not AI, are accountable. This stance aligns with President Donald Trump's opposition to regulatory crackdowns on the AI industry, which he supports expanding in the U.S. despite some AI leaders calling for a slowdown due to risks.

Bessent also discussed his recent 12-hour meeting with Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng, where they talked about AI cooperation and the possibility of establishing communication channels to address AI-related risks. The talks occurred ahead of a summit between Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping and included discussions on the upcoming expiration of the U.S.-China trade truce and other geopolitical issues.

items.title: Ron Johnson, Apple retail pioneer, doubts AI agents will replace in-store shopping experience despite Silicon Valley's push [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: The man who built Apple’s stores doesn’t buy Silicon Valley’s bet on AI shopping
items.summary:
Ron Johnson, who built Apple's retail stores, expressed skepticism about Silicon Valley's heavy investment in AI-driven shopping, arguing that physical stores and human interaction remain essential for many purchases. He emphasized that while AI can enhance online shopping by informing consumers, it cannot replicate the tactile experience and personal judgment involved in buying products like laptops.

Johnson highlighted that Apple's retail success was rooted in its focus on people and customer service rather than technology alone, noting that employees are not paid on commission to foster genuine customer care. Despite his doubts about AI replacing physical retail, Johnson remains optimistic about AI's potential to improve shopping experiences without substituting human intuition.

items.originalTitle: ArtifactBench: Evaluating AI Music Detectors Under Distribution Shift
items.summary:
ArtifactBench is a new evaluation suite designed to measure the performance of AI-generated music detectors considering generator lineage, source provenance, and audio transformations. It separates calibration from testing, tracks inference failures, and reports source-level performance with uncertainty, addressing limitations of aggregate benchmark scores.

The benchmark was used to assess multiple public detectors under a standardized protocol, revealing significant performance differences and exposing generator- and domain-specific shifts that aggregate metrics conceal. For example, ArtifactNet achieved 0.982 AUROC and 0.918 balanced accuracy on a common test set, outperforming other detectors like Deezer, SpecTTTra, and CLAM, which showed lower accuracy under shifted cohorts.

items.title: Researchers report two sandbox escapes in OpenAI Codex, both fixed within eight days, exposing risks in code execution restrictions [ * ] [ ⬢ ]
items.originalTitle: Escaping the OpenAI Codex sandbox, twice
items.summary:
Researchers discovered two vulnerabilities in the OpenAI Codex sandbox environment that allowed code execution beyond intended restrictions. The first, called Overpatch, exploited a patch tool to gain write access to the entire disk without approval. The second, Heapjack, involved untrusted JavaScript code reading a secret token from shared memory to execute commands outside the sandbox in read-only mode. Both issues were reported to OpenAI on August 12, 2026, and patched within eight days.

The Overpatch vulnerability arose because the patch tool granted write permissions based on input paths, enabling writes outside the designated workspace. Heapjack exploited the shared memory between trusted and untrusted contexts in a Node.js process, allowing untrusted code to extract a secret token and perform unsandboxed operations. These findings highlight the challenges of enforcing sandbox boundaries when enforcement mechanisms reside within the same environment they protect.

To address such risks, the researchers developed Accomplish, a system that runs the entire agent inside a virtual machine with strict isolation, preventing untrusted code from accessing real credentials or executing unauthorized actions on the host system. This approach treats all code inside the VM as untrusted, ensuring sandbox enforcement is external to the environment it governs.

items.originalTitle: Amazon blocks Meta's Muse AI assistant
items.summary:
Amazon has blocked Meta's Muse AI assistant from accessing its e-commerce site after Meta did not inform Amazon or obtain permission for Muse to shop on its platform. Amazon cited concerns that Muse does not identify itself when browsing and may capture customer credentials, posing privacy and security risks. The company displayed a message warning users that unauthorized AI agent access violates its Conditions of Use.

The dispute highlights tensions between the two companies, which have existing partnerships including Amazon products being purchasable on Facebook and Instagram and Meta running AI workloads on Amazon's cloud infrastructure. Amazon has previously taken legal and technical measures to block other AI shopping agents, emphasizing the importance of merchant consent and customer safety in automated purchasing.

Amazon is in direct talks with Meta about the issue but has not ruled out legal action. The case raises broader questions about control over online shopping experiences and the responsibilities of AI agents acting on behalf of consumers.

items.originalTitle: China's AI Realism Is Not Conspiracy
items.summary:
An article challenges the notion that Chinese AI researchers' perspectives on US AI policies are conspiracy-driven, arguing instead that their views are grounded in realist assessments of interstate competition. It highlights that Chinese researchers, many with US academic or professional experience, interpret US export controls and AI safety discourse as strategic moves to maintain national advantage rather than propaganda.

The piece contrasts this with Western interpretations that often dismiss Chinese views as radical or conspiratorial, emphasizing that Chinese researchers' conclusions stem from direct observation of US technology industry behavior and policy changes. It also discusses the perceived contradictions in US AI policy positions, such as restricting China's AI development while seeking regulatory cooperation, which Chinese researchers find insulting and indicative of underlying strategic competition.

items.title: StClair.ai argues AI chat windows provide poor user experience and proposes HTML-based interfaces for more functional, interactive AI interactions [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: We're Using AI Wrong. The Chat Window Sucks
items.summary:
The article critiques the traditional AI chat window interface as inefficient and difficult to navigate, likening it to an endless, unsearchable stream of information. It proposes using local HTML documents as interactive AI interfaces, allowing users to work more effectively by integrating AI directly into familiar document formats.

The author introduces Lahe, a tool combining a local server and JavaScript to create live, editable HTML documents that serve as AI interfaces. This approach enables features like collapsible sidebars, multi-tab AI agents, and actionable to-do lists, reducing task switching and improving workflow. The article highlights how this method leverages decades of web UX design to enhance AI usability beyond simple chat interactions.

items.originalTitle: OpenAI forms math advisory group as its AI resolves more than 100 open problems
items.summary:
OpenAI announced the creation of an independent Advisory Group on Mathematics and Artificial Intelligence hosted at the Institute for Advanced Study in Princeton to provide mathematicians input on the company’s math research. This follows OpenAI’s AI model resolving more than 100 open problems, including the Navier-Stokes Millennium Prize problem.

The advisory group will assess the significance of new results and coordinate their release but will not have authority to slow or redirect OpenAI’s ongoing mathematical research. Members can offer advice and public views independently, but decision-making responsibility remains with OpenAI.

items.title: California Gov. Gavin Newsom signs seven bills requiring AI data centers to pay for local energy grid and water system upgrades and disclose resource use [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: California tightens rules on AI data center energy and water use
items.summary:
California Governor Gavin Newsom has signed a package of seven bills aimed at regulating AI data centers' energy and water consumption. The laws require the California Public Utilities Commission to create a new rate classification for data centers and mandate that these centers pay for necessary upgrades to local power grids and water systems to prevent utility costs from being passed onto residents.

The legislation also obliges proposed data centers to disclose estimated water usage, energy efficiency, and drought planning information to local governments. Additionally, data centers must meet specific energy, water, and fuel consumption standards to qualify for streamlined approval processes. This move follows Newsom's recent executive order to accelerate the development of an AI "kill switch."

items.title: Meta’s Muse AI app surpasses ChatGPT in downloads and daily active users in U.S. and Canada during first 12 days [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Meta’s Muse is outpacing ChatGPT’s early mobile launch
items.summary:
Meta’s new AI app Muse has outpaced ChatGPT’s early mobile launch in the U.S. and Canada, achieving 1.8 million downloads compared to ChatGPT’s 1.3 million in the same 12-day period, according to market intelligence firm Apptopia. Muse also has higher daily active users, with 642,000 in the U.S. versus ChatGPT’s 231,000 at the same point after launch.

Muse is available on both iOS and Android but limited to the U.S. and Canada, while ChatGPT launched globally on iOS only. Apptopia’s comparison focuses on iOS data in these markets to align the figures. Muse has climbed to the No. 1 spot on the U.S. App Store, surpassing ChatGPT, and benefits from integration with Meta’s platforms like Facebook, Instagram, and WhatsApp, which likely supports its growth.

Meta has not publicly shared internal adoption figures for Muse. The app’s early success suggests it could become a significant addition to Meta’s portfolio, following the company’s previous success with Instagram’s Threads, which leveraged cross-promotion across Meta’s ecosystem to reach over 500 million users.

items.title: MIT Technology Review outlines four recommendations to address failures in US border surveillance towers after investigation reveals undetected migrant deaths [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: 4 ways to address the failures we found along the US border’s “virtual wall”
items.summary:
MIT Technology Review published an investigation revealing that advanced AI-enabled surveillance towers along the US-Mexico border have failed to detect many migrants who later died nearby, exposing systemic flaws such as broken equipment, ineffective algorithms, and unresponsive agents. The report highlights over 1,050 deaths near these towers and calls for urgent reforms in border surveillance practices.

The investigation, part of a collaboration with Times of San Diego, found that US Customs and Border Protection (CBP) has never conducted a comprehensive audit of the towers' effectiveness or tracked migrant deaths systematically. The report recommends a thorough audit of deaths near the virtual wall, improved tracking of migrant deaths and remains, and better documentation of cases where surveillance technology leads to apprehensions. These steps aim to address the shortcomings in the current $1 billion federal investment to expand the virtual wall by 2034.

The findings raise concerns about the accountability and efficacy of border security technology, especially as defense contractor Anduril continues to secure major contracts for new towers. The report underscores the need for CBP to implement data-driven oversight and transparency measures to prevent further loss of life and improve rescue efforts along the border.

items.title: Researchers find zero-day vulnerability in Meta's Muse AI assistant allowing local apps full control, raising security concerns [ ! ] [ ⬢ ]
items.originalTitle: Muse, Meta's extraordinarily privileged AI assistant, has a serious 0-day
items.summary:
Meta's AI assistant Muse, designed to manage tasks and access user accounts on macOS, has a zero-day vulnerability that lets any local app or terminal command gain full control over the assistant by accessing its authentication token. The flaw stems from design choices allowing apps to modify sensitive settings, including the transcription endpoint, enabling attackers to redirect data and hijack the assistant.

Security expert Patrick Wardle demonstrated proof-of-concept attacks exploiting this vulnerability to perform actions like writing malicious files and taking pictures without user alerts. Meta has not responded to inquiries, and Amazon has blocked Muse from its site, citing violations of its conditions of use. The incident raises questions about the security and privacy measures implemented in Muse, especially given its extensive access to user data and device resources.

items.title: Researchers introduce BI-Agent and BI-Bench to automate end-to-end business intelligence workflows using large language models and tool-augmented reasoning [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: BI-Agent and BI-Bench: Towards Automating End-to-End Business Intelligence
items.summary:
Researchers have developed BI-Agent, a tool-augmented system designed to automate complex business intelligence (BI) workflows by decomposing tasks such as data search, join, and transformation. They also created BI-Bench, the first benchmark dataset derived from real-world BI projects, to evaluate large language models' (LLMs) ability to answer BI questions end-to-end without manual data preparation. Initial tests showed that even advanced LLMs perform below 50% accuracy on BI-Bench, highlighting the challenge of automating BI tasks fully with existing models.

To improve performance, the team applied supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning to BI-Agent using synthesized training trajectories from real BI projects, achieving accuracy gains of up to 40 percentage points with vanilla LLMs and further improvements with post-training. Their findings emphasize the importance of combining domain-specific post-training with tool-augmented reasoning to enhance LLM capabilities in complex BI workflows and suggest promising directions for future research in automating enterprise decision-making processes.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2609.20886v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Business intelligence (BI) is a cornerstone of enterprise decision-making and is widely used by enterprise users in software such as Power BI and Tableau. In traditional BI workflows, users need to prepare data by (1) identifying relevant tables, (2) performing data transformations, and (3) building join relationships, before they can (4) answer their business questions. These steps can be complex and time-consuming, making BI challenging. Given the strong capabilities of large language models (LLMs) in working with data, we study their ability to answer BI questions end-to-end, without requiring users to manually perform the tedious preparation steps. To do this, we harvest a large collection of real-world BI projects from public sources, and manually extract pairs of (questions, ground-truth answers) from real user dashboards. The resulting benchmark, BI-Bench, is the first benchmark to systematically study LLMs' ability on end-to-end BI. We find that even frontier LLMs perform poorly on BI-Bench, with less than 50% accuracy. To address their limitations, we design a tool-augmented BI-Agent that decomposes BI workflows into subtasks on structured data, such as search, join, and transform, and orchestrates specialized data management methods across BI stages. Furthermore, we develop a post-training framework that synthesizes training trajectories from real BI projects, enabling BI-Agent to be further post-trained using both supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and reinforcement learning (RL). BI-Agent achieves substantial accuracy gains of up to 40 percentage points with vanilla LLMs, and post-trained BI-Agent yields gains of up to 30 points. Our results highlight the importance of combining tool-augmented reasoning with domain-specific post-training in complex BI workflows, and point to promising directions for future research.

items.title: Researchers show multi-agent test-time communication outperforms independent agents on complex problem-solving benchmarks, with gains scaling by team size [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Scaling Discovery through Test-Time Communication
items.summary:
Researchers demonstrate that teams of communicating AI agents significantly outperform independent agents on challenging tasks requiring novel problem solving, such as the ARC-AGI-3 benchmark. A team of k communicating agents matches the success rate of 4k independent agents, and this advantage grows with team size, enabling solutions to tasks no single agent can solve alone. These benefits extend to research-oriented tasks like polyomino packing and MNIST classifier compression, where communicating agents surpass prior best-known results, including human solutions.

The study finds that these gains depend on sufficient computational resources and clear feedback; under limited compute or ambiguous progress measures, independent agents may perform better. The communication occurs via a shared directory without predefined roles, highlighting the potential of collaborative AI systems to scale discovery and problem solving beyond isolated efforts.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2609.21032v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Science advances not in isolation but through collaboration, yet existing agentic systems capture little of this. Whether communicating agents help remains an open question with mixed prior results. We show that test-time communication can substantially outperform independent parallel attempts on challenging tasks, where sharing a breakthrough can push the whole group forward. We first study the effect of scaling multi-agent test-time communication, where agents have no predefined roles and communicate via a shared directory, on ARC-AGI-3, a benchmark requiring novel problem solving. We find that a team of $k$ communicating agents, team@$k$, matches the success rate of $4k$ independent agents, and this advantage grows with $k$, suggesting gains compound with scale. The effect is not merely efficiency: a task that no single agent can solve, a team of agents can solve reliably. Furthermore, these gains transfer to research-oriented tasks, given sufficient compute. On polyomino packing, communicating agents outperform best@$k$ and exceed the prior best-known score. On MNIST classifier compression, communication surpasses the best-known human solution. A team of four agents produced a 1,957-byte classifier submission achieving 99.4% test accuracy, smaller than both the best-known human solution and the best single-agent result. These gains are not unconditional. Independent agents may outperform communication when compute is limited or when a clear measure of progress is absent. However, under sufficient compute and clear feedback, multi-agent communication consistently yields stronger results.

items.title: Researchers analyze attention graph topology to detect hallucinations in large language models, linking impaired context sharing to hallucination patterns [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Detecting Hallucination in LLMs: Tracing the Topological Signatures of Impaired Context Sharing
items.summary:
Researchers examine the topology of information flow within attention graphs to distinguish hallucinated from non-hallucinated responses in large language models (LLMs). They use Forman-Ricci curvature to identify structural patterns indicating information bottlenecks and introduce a method capturing both semi-local and global information-flow characteristics of attention heads associated with hallucinations. Their approach shows consistent improvements over existing baselines across multiple hallucination-detection benchmarks and diverse LLM architectures.

Further analysis reveals that hallucinations in LLMs are strongly associated with impaired context sharing among tokens during causal generation. Hallucinated responses tend to exhibit over-reliance on self-attention, diffused context retrieval from earlier tokens, or information over-squashing, particularly in the final transformer layer.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2609.21096v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this work, we examine the topology of information flow patterns within attention graphs to effectively distinguish hallucinated from non-hallucinated responses. We analyze the Forman-Ricci curvature to identify structural patterns indicating information bottlenecks in attention graphs. We then introduce a method that captures both semi-local and global information-flow characteristics of attention heads associated with hallucinated responses. We evaluate our approach extensively across several LLMs and established benchmarks. Empirical results demonstrate that our proposed single-pass approach provides consistent improvements over existing attention-based and multi-response baselines across two hallucination-detection benchmarks, while achieving competitive performance across diverse LLM architectures. Further analysis reveals that impaired context sharing among tokens during causal generation is strongly associated with hallucination occurrences in LLMs. In particular, hallucinated responses are consistently characterized by an over-reliance on self-attention, diffused context retrieval from earlier tokens, or information over-squashing, especially in the final transformer layer.

items.title: Researchers introduce Energy Transfer Detection method to improve pretraining data detection in large language models using a free-energy perspective [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Detecting Pretraining Data in Large Language Models from a Free-Energy Perspective
items.summary:
Detecting pretraining data in large language models is difficult because high likelihood scores can indicate either prior training exposure or strong generalization. Researchers propose a new method called Energy Transfer Detection (ETD) that adjusts prediction loss relative to predictive entropy, improving the separation between training data members and non-members. This approach interprets the detection problem through a Helmholtz free-energy framework, enhancing detection accuracy and robustness across various settings.

The ETD method uses an inclined boundary in the joint space of prediction loss and predictive entropy, reducing variance in membership signals and extending analysis to cases with nonzero entropy gaps. Experiments demonstrate that ETD outperforms previous detectors, increasing average AUROC by up to 3.5% and true positive rate at 5% false positive rate by up to 5.1%, indicating more reliable identification of pretraining data in large language models.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2609.21888v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Detecting pretraining data in large language models is challenging because high likelihood can reflect either training exposure or strong generalization. In the joint space of prediction loss and predictive entropy, a likelihood-only detector uses a horizontal boundary and can mistake predictable non-members for members. Motivated by this, we introduce an inclined boundary that evaluates prediction loss relative to predictive entropy. Our analysis shows that entropy correction can preserve the expected membership signal while reducing its variance, thereby improving standardized member--non-member separation. We further extend the mean--variance analysis to the more general setting with a nonzero mean entropy gap. Interestingly, this entropy-adjusted score admits a Helmholtz free-energy interpretation, leading to Energy Transfer Detection (ETD), which views pretraining data detection from a macroscopic residual free-energy transfer perspective. Extensive experiments show that ETD achieves the best average detection performance, improving average AUROC by up to 3.5\% and TPR@5\%FPR by up to 5.1\%, while remaining robust across diverse settings.

items.title: Researchers find LLMs compute verbal confidence automatically during answer generation and cache it for later retrieval, reflecting sophisticated self-evaluation beyond token probabilities [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: How do LLMs Compute Verbal Confidence
items.summary:
A new study investigates how large language models (LLMs) generate verbal confidence scores, which are used to estimate uncertainty. The research shows that models like Gemma 3 27B, Qwen 2.5 7B, and Magistral Small 24B compute confidence automatically during answer generation, cache it immediately after the answer, and retrieve it for verbalization rather than computing it on demand. This cached confidence reflects a richer evaluation of answer quality rather than just token log-probabilities.

The study uses techniques such as activation steering, patching, noising, and attention blocking to trace the flow of confidence information within the models. Linear probing and variance partitioning reveal that cached confidence representations explain significant variance in verbal confidence outputs, indicating that LLMs perform an automatic, sophisticated self-assessment. These findings have implications for understanding metacognition in LLMs and improving their calibration.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2603.17839v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Verbal confidence -- prompting LLMs to state their confidence as a number or category -- is widely used to extract uncertainty estimates from black-box models. However, how LLMs internally generate such scores remains unknown. We address two questions: first, when confidence is computed -- just-in-time when requested, or automatically during answer generation and cached for later retrieval; and second, what verbal confidence represents -- token log-probabilities, or a richer evaluation of answer quality? Focusing on Gemma 3 27B (across TriviaQA, BigMath, and MMLU), Qwen 2.5 7B, and the reasoning model Magistral Small 24B, we provide convergent evidence for cached retrieval. Activation steering, patching, noising, and swap experiments reveal that confidence representations emerge at answer-adjacent positions before appearing at the verbalization site. Attention blocking pinpoints the information flow: confidence is gathered from answer tokens, cached at the first post-answer position, then retrieved for output. Critically, linear probing and variance partitioning reveal that these cached representations explain substantial variance in verbal confidence beyond token log-probabilities, suggesting a richer answer-quality evaluation rather than a simple fluency readout. These findings demonstrate that verbal confidence reflects automatic, sophisticated self-evaluation -- not post-hoc reconstruction -- with implications for understanding metacognition in LLMs and improving calibration.

items.title: Researchers analyze how transformer models perform few-shot addition tasks via localized attention head activation subspaces [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Understanding In-context Learning of Addition via Activation Subspaces
items.summary: Researchers studied how modern transformer language models implement few-shot learning for addition tasks by analyzing activation subspaces in attention heads. They found that a small number of attention heads in models like Llama-3-8B-Instruct encode addition rules using low-dimensional subspaces that track digits and magnitude through trigonometric and low-frequency components. The study also derived a mathematical identity linking subspaces responsible for aggregating and extracting information, providing insight into the internal computation of few-shot learning in transformers. This approach generalizes to other arithmetic and semantic tasks, and the researchers have made their code publicly available.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2505.05145v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: To perform few-shot learning, language models extract signals from a few input-label pairs, aggregate them into a learned prediction rule, and apply this rule to new inputs. How is this implemented in the forward pass of modern transformer models? To explore this question, we study a structured family of few-shot learning tasks for which the true prediction rule is to add an integer $k$ to the input. We introduce a novel method that localizes the model's few-shot learning ability to only a few attention heads. This method and the findings generalize to four additional task families spanning arithmetic and semantic tasks. We then perform an in-depth analysis of individual heads via dimensionality reduction and decomposition of the heads' output spaces. For example, in Llama-3-8B-Instruct, we reduce the mechanism underlying these tasks to just three attention heads with six-dimensional subspaces, in which four dimensions track the units digit using trigonometric functions with periods $2$, $5$, and $10$, while two dimensions track magnitude using low-frequency components. To deepen our understanding of this mechanism, we also derive a mathematical identity relating the ''aggregator'' and ''extractor'' subspaces of attention heads, allowing us to track the flow of information from individual examples to a final aggregated concept. Our results demonstrate how tracking low-dimensional subspaces of localized heads throughout a forward pass can provide insight into fine-grained computational structures in language models. Our code is available at https://github.com/xyVickyHu/addition-subspaces.

items.originalTitle: Teaching LLMs to Self-Evolve: Cultivating Core Meta-Skills with Reinforcement Learning
items.summary: Researchers present MetaEvolve, a framework that cultivates meta-skills like self-reflection and iterative refinement in large language models using a data synthesis pipeline, evolution-aware reinforcement learning, and evolutionary search at inference time. Grounded in coding tasks where program execution provides continuous reward signals, MetaEvolve trains models on evolution trajectories combining correctness and efficiency scores. Across seven coding benchmarks, it outperforms strong baselines by 10.01% on in-distribution tasks and 24.12% on out-of-distribution tasks, achieving a 46.9% improvement on algorithm optimization problems outside the training domain. These results suggest that explicitly training LLMs to self-evolve can lead to more capable and autonomous AI systems.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.21971v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Test-time scaling through iterative self-evolution with environment feedback, as demonstrated by AlphaEvolve, shows remarkable performance gains. We hypothesize that the success of such evolution frameworks hinges on meta-skills, such as self-reflection with environment feedback, that enable effective multi-round refinement, yet are largely neglected by traditional post-training. To bridge this gap, we present MetaEvolve, a framework designed to develop these meta-skills via a data synthesis pipeline, evolution-aware reinforcement learning (RL), and inference-time evolutionary search. Concretely, we ground MetaEvolve in coding, where program execution provides natural, continuous reward signals beyond binary correctness. Building on these signals, we synthesize evolution trajectories as training data, each containing a current program, its fitness score (combining correctness and efficiency), and a history of prior attempts, and train the model via RL with verifiable rewards derived from test case execution. By training on large-scale code data, we aim to inspire generalizable domain-agnostic meta-skills that can transfer broadly to open-ended problems where such rich training signals are scarce. Across seven coding benchmarks, MetaEvolve outperforms the strongest baseline by 10.01% absolute on in-distribution tasks and 24.12% on out-of-distribution tasks. On open-ended algorithm optimization problems entirely outside the training domain, it further achieves a 46.9% relative improvement. These results demonstrate that explicitly cultivating self-evolution meta-skills offers a principled path toward more capable and autonomously self-evolving AI.

items.title: Researchers introduce Balance of Benchmarks framework for task-conditioned model comparison using semantic density reweighting and score equating across diverse benchmarks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Balance of Benchmarks: Semantic Density Reweighting for Task-Conditioned Model Comparison
items.summary:
Researchers present Balance of Benchmarks (BoB), a framework designed to improve model comparison by adjusting the influence of benchmark scores based on semantic density and task relevance, using only publicly available aggregate scores. BoB addresses limitations of uniform averaging and manual benchmark curation by combining semantic density weighting, score equating across benchmarks of varying difficulty, and task-relevant residual pooling.

The framework was evaluated on 605 configurations across 14 Artificial Analysis benchmarks and on WildScores, a collection of 148 developer-reported benchmarks. BoB-Support improved family-mean Spearman correlation from 0.764 to 0.823, reduced mean absolute error from 6.19 to 5.10 normalized score points, and increased three-model shortlist hit rate from 65.3% to 72.6%. BoB-Constant achieved a Spearman correlation of 0.831 and a hit rate of 74.6%. Additionally, density weighting reduced ranking changes when benchmarks were repeated or paraphrased, and BoB-Support lowered retrospective shortlist regret. The framework makes benchmark inclusion, redundancy, and task relevance explicit and testable, enabling fuller use of existing benchmark evidence while moderating the impact of benchmark proliferation.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2608.30044v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Model comparison increasingly relies on large collections of publicly reported benchmark scores, yet common aggregation strategies trade off evidence coverage against control over capability weighting. Manually curated suites leave potentially informative evaluations unused, while uniform averaging retains them but gives greater influence to capabilities that happen to be benchmarked more densely. We introduce Balance of Benchmarks (BoB), a framework that retains eligible benchmark evidence while adapting its influence for task-conditioned model comparison using only public aggregate scores. BoB combines semantic density weighting, score equating across benchmarks of different difficulty, and task-relevant residual pooling. We evaluate it on 605 configurations across 14 Artificial Analysis benchmarks and on WildScores, a collection of 148 developer-reported benchmarks evaluated with held-out source-lineage families. On WildScores, BoB-Support raises family-mean Spearman correlation from 0.764 under uniform standardized averaging to 0.823, reduces MAE from 6.19 to 5.10 normalized score points, and increases three-model shortlist hit rate from 65.3% to 72.6%. BoB-Constant reaches a Spearman correlation of 0.831 and a hit rate of 74.6%. Separately, density weighting reduces average ranking changes when benchmarks are repeated, including as paraphrased copies. BoB-Support also reduces retrospective three-model shortlist regret from 2.08 to 1.67 normalized score points. BoB makes benchmark inclusion, redundancy, and task relevance explicit and testable measurement choices, allowing existing benchmark evidence to be used more fully while moderating the influence of benchmark proliferation.

items.title: Researchers present LGM, a neuro-symbolic framework for disentangling long-term memory in personalized agents using latent graph construction and query-aware relational weights [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Disentangling Long-Term Memory via Latent Neuro-Symbolic Reasoning
items.summary:
Researchers introduce LGM, a novel neuro-symbolic framework designed to improve personalized agents' reasoning over long-term interaction histories by disentangling memory in a continuous latent space. The approach uses a sparse autoencoder to map historical interactions into latent memory nodes and dynamically synthesizes query-aware relational edge weights, enabling more expressive memory representations.

LGM replaces fixed graph structures with tailored latent graphs conditioned on each query, allowing non-linear message passing directed by query embeddings. Experiments on long-term personalization benchmarks show that LGM outperforms state-of-the-art methods in capturing both explicit and implicit user preferences, facilitating more effective personalized responses.

LGM replaces fixed graph structures with tailored latent graphs conditioned on each query, allowing non-linear message passing directed by query embeddings. items.originalSummary: arXiv:2609.18461v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Personalized agents are required to reason over long-term history interactions to infer both explicit preferences and implicit behavioral evidence. While early flat retrieval methods score memory fragments independently and neglect the distributed information, current structured memory frameworks rely on query-agnostic static graphs that fail to capture the context-dependent relations. Crucially, raw textual memories are inherently entangled and noisy, making fine-grained personalization and cross-session reasoning computationally prohibitive. To this end, we present LGM, a novel neuro-symbolic framework that shifts long-term memory disentanglement into a continuous latent space. Specifically, (i) instead of persisting fixed graphs, we design a tailored latent graph construction with a sparse autoencoder. Subject to each query, it maps historical interactions into latent memory nodes and disentangles the memory traces into sparse concept activations, dynamically synthesizing query-aware relational edge weights. (ii) A graph encoder then treats the query embedding as a conditioning preference to direct non-linear message passing across the task-specific latent subgraph. This yields a highly expressive memory representation for effective activations. Extensive experiments on long-term personalization benchmarks demonstrate that LGM significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baselines in capturing both explicit and implicit preferences while enabling personalized responses.

items.title: OpenAI Develops Features to Counter Grok Bot, Mulls Response to Meta’s Muse [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: OpenAI Develops Features to Counter Grok Bot, Mulls Response to Meta’s Muse
items.summary:
OpenAI pioneered AI that can take over web browsers and other applications on people’s behalf, and its ChatGPT app brought generative AI to consumers. Now that rivals like SpaceX and Meta are pushing the boundaries by launching personal AI agents that handle multistep tasks, OpenAI is playing catch-up.

For instance, OpenAI is developing features to compete more directly with SpaceX’s recently launched Grok Bot, which helps customers create always-on AI “teammates” to handle routine tasks, manage software, and collaborate in the background, according to a person with knowledge of the effort. OpenAI also has discussed developing a personal AI assistant to compete with one that Meta Platforms recently launched, according to another person with knowledge of the situation.

In developing such products, OpenAI would be repurposing and rebranding some of the existing “agentic” technology it already offers through Codex and ChatGPT. Some customers of these OpenAI apps have already connected them to their email, calendar and other applications so they can automate tasks such as scheduling appointments or communicating with businesses by email, sometimes over multiple days.

items.originalTitle: CrowdStrike and Okta Trade at Big Premiums Despite Unproven AI Payoff
items.summary:
Cybersecurity stocks have enjoyed a good run in 2026 as investors bet on the idea that they’ll benefit from companies shoring up their defenses against AI-fueled online threats. The S&P Kensho cybersecurity index is up 41% this year compared to an 11% rise in the S&P 500 over the same period.

But some of the names attracting the most interest, such as cloud-based security firm CrowdStrike and identity security software provider Okta, have soared to valuation highs that should give investors in the sector pause. So far, there’s limited evidence that their revenue growth is getting a boost from new AI concerns.

items.title: The Real Cost of AI: A Survey of the Unpredictable Token Economics [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: The Real Cost of AI: A Survey of the Unpredictable Token Economics
items.summary:
For decades, enterprise software budgeting was a predictable exercise: negotiate a subscription fee, project the number of seats you need, move on. AI has broken that model. Pricing tied to tokens — the metered unit behind most AI billing — has turned technology spend into a variable cost, and an unpredictable one.

The Information’s survey of 107 of our readers - senior leaders and professionals (See Methodology) - finds that most companies haven’t gotten a handle on it: 60% say the cost trajectory of their AI initiatives is unpredictable, at the exact moment CFOs, boards and investors are demanding proof of ROI.

60%: “The cost trajectory of AI initiatives is unpredictable.”

This piece draws on that survey and The Information’s Deep Research to examine where AI budgets are actually going, why token costs remain so hard to forecast, and what separates the companies that have managed AI spending from those still being surprised by their bills.

The Bulk of the AI Budget

Outside the hyperscalers, who are pouring billions into data centers, most companies put the bulk of their AI investment — 64% — into software, applications, and API models. (See Chart.) That reflects where ROI is actually realized, according to The Information: most businesses want solutions to specific problems, not infrastructure to manage.

This 64% budget line includes the unpredictability factor, the token, which behaves unlike anything else in the technology budget.

Let’s unpack the costs of different types of software. The classic subscription/SaaS model relies on per-seat licenses for enterprise systems of record and the cloud services that underpin them, such as CRM (Salesforce), ERP/HR and finance (SAP, Workday), and collaboration (Slack).

Packaged AI apps and assistants, like ChatGPT or Microsoft Copilot, are also largely bought per seat. The flat seat price covers token usage but also limits what an AI assistant can do. The main drawback of seat-based licensing has always been waste: many paid seats sit idle or underused.

The token consumption appears in the AI layer of independent digital agents that perform complex tasks rather than simply answering a query. These agents use metered, token-based pricing that scales with usage, making forecasting much harder, and they consume far more compute than basic chatbots.

As AI shifts from chatbots to autonomous agents running in the background, the companies least practiced at controlling token usage are seeing the biggest surprises on their bills. That’s because such agents operate in loops, and a single inefficient prompt can snowball very quickly.

For routine data manipulation and established workflows, traditional software is often still cheaper and more reliable than agentic AI. When budget predictability matters most, AI’s consumption-based pricing is a liability, not a feature.

One survey respondent frames it as a balancing act: “We should be looking for the best of both worlds. Even with a reasonably implemented, small, hosted cloud environment, the cost per transaction for software is nothing like that of pure agent workloads. The cost of going to pure AI can be prohibitive. There must be a balance among human decisions, programmed software, and pure AI.”

The Intersection of Token Consumption and Productivity

Reader experience with AI productivity varies widely — even within the same industry. One respondent building a startup says, “With my agentic AI assistant, I am compressing what took me 3 years to build into 6 months.” A technology lawyer at a large enterprise draws a much tighter line, restricting AI to coding and software-vulnerability remediation. AI is useful for legal research, this reader says, but “the amount of quality control that I have to do with AI-generated content adds to the frustration I feel when having to explain to management why AI can’t solve all our problems.”

Despite the variance, respondents were broadly positive on ROI: 60% say AI increases productivity, more than half say it returns more than it costs, and nearly half report lower internal labor costs. (See Chart)

The intersection of “token economics” and workforce productivity has confounded business leaders and accounting departments. First, some companies have equated token consumption with productivity, a mistake. Token consumption itself is not a proxy for a worker’s productivity. More tokens don’t necessarily mean a better outcome. On the contrary, they can cause AI agents to loop, generating large volumes of responses that can run up compute costs and overwhelm a human.

The crux of the issue is translating token consumption into productivity – not equating the two. Token consumption is an input, not an output. It’s the compute era’s equivalent of billable hours: easy to count, weakly correlated with value. Measure outcomes, not token metrics, with the caveat that outcomes are much harder to measure than tokens.

Some metrics that are more useful than tokens to consider include task-completion units (the emerging standard), which count the tasks completed by its agents rather than the tokens processed; cycle-time compression for a given process; and revenue or cost attribution.

AI Adoption and Regulatory Compliance

“Regulatory compliance is slowing us down” has become one of the most common explanations for sluggish AI adoption. The smallest share of survey respondents, 17%, view regulatory compliance as an accelerant for AI adoption.

As government regulations, data privacy laws, and corporate governance requirements increase, the cost to develop, run, and use AI rises significantly. Ensuring that AI acts safely and complies with enterprise parameters requires more “thinking” and therefore more tokens. This is largely because ensuring that models, especially agentic models, are secure, compliant, and safe requires immense computational overhead.

While legal uncertainty and the number of regulations are genuine concerns, large companies also face the buildout of AI bureaucracy, including chief AI officers, adoption dashboards, token budgets or governance councils, according to The Information. This bureaucracy is a mechanism to deploy AI at scale but it also obscures whether any of it pays for itself. The economics of AI, especially in the era of tokenization, can be confusing and the AI bureaucracy itself is not its cause but its symptom.

Common flaws of AI governance include companies governing AI at the policy layer (committees, principles, training) while risk lives at the identity and permission layer. Most policy frameworks are written as instruction sets delivered to the AI model, while the controls that work (deterministic triggers, permission gates, scoped credentials) are enforced outside the model. On top of that, companies may not always know what they are governing, as vendors and employees are adding shadow AI features.

The right approach inverts the framing most companies start with. The default assumption is a tradeoff — compliance slows adoption, so minimize one to maximize the other. The evidence points the other way: the things blocking adoption are the compliance questions, and the companies moving fastest are the ones that resolved them first. But before doing it fast, they must do it right.

Token Cost Management

Token cost management is where the survey’s biggest paradox appears. A slim majority of companies (52%) say they understand token costs, and about as many know that disciplined prompt and output engineering can substantially reduce them. Yet only about a third say they actually control token costs in practice. (See Chart)

“Token cost management is not yet in line with the growth in usage of AI,” one respondent writes.

Only one in five respondents (20%) believe that buying tokens in higher volumes lowers cost-per-query (see Chart). Yet The Information’s research shows that batching purchases is an effective and increasingly necessary strategy for cutting per-query costs on frontier models, which carry a steep premium over simpler ones. Equally important for savings is selecting token-guzzling frontier models only for tasks that require them.

The Information’s research and reader responses point to five ways companies are managing token costs:

  1. Train users. Teach employees about model selection, how to prevent models from overthinking, and how to prompt and structure requests to achieve the most useful output at the lowest token cost. Also, teach employees when not to use AI.
  2. Match the right model to the right task. Route routine queries to cheaper, open-source models and reserve frontier models for genuinely complex reasoning. “If you select the models best aligned with most tasks, token costs are incredibly low. All the news about token costs concerns frontier models, which are rarely required,” one respondent writes.
  3. Optimize prompts. Keep them concise, strip unnecessary context, and reuse outputs where possible. The Information’s research shows that these “token-minimizing” techniques are being deployed to reduce the volume of data a model must process per request.
  4. Cap and track usage. Track token usage against productivity, not just spend, and set daily or weekly caps when usage is outpacing value. At one respondent’s company, employees don’t have unfettered access to tokens: “Only authorized employees may use tokens, following a defined mandate and an allocated development budget based on a cost-benefit analysis.”
  5. Adopt a systemic approach. Some respondents argue that the fix isn’t behavioral at all. “Cost efficiency is largely determined by systemic, deterministic constraints, rather than individuals voluntarily enforcing constraints upon themselves,” one respondent writes. A systemic approach includes creating a single controlled AI gateway (eradicating shadow AI), introducing hard spend ceilings with approval gates, and making the cheapest path automatic.

Looking Ahead

AI is getting more expensive, not less. The shift from chatbots to autonomous agents built for multi-step workflows is the single biggest driver of rising costs, and token-based pricing means uncontrolled usage shows up directly on the bill. Respondents expect that trend to continue: most see AI-related spending rising across the board over the next 12 months. (See Chart)

That’s happening as the enterprise AI market moves past its experimental phase and into one where spending gets scrutinized like any other line item. Companies that haven’t yet built model routing, usage limits, and hard budget caps into their AI programs are likely to keep absorbing costs they can’t fully explain.

Methodology

Based on a survey of 107 senior leaders and professionals, conducted in June and July 2026.

Company size: Forty-five percent of companies surveyed had revenues under $10 million; 20% had revenues of more than $1 billion; 16% had revenues between $10 million and $100 million; 12% had revenues between $100 million and $500 million, and 8% had revenues between $500 million and $1 billion.

Key industry sectors: Thirty-eight percent of companies were from technology, media and telecommunications; 13% from professional services; 10% from healthcare and life sciences; 9% from financial services & capital markets, and the remaining 29% came from the government, retail, public sector and others.

Respondent titles and roles: Forty percent were executive leadership (including CEOs, CIOs and CTOs) and owners; 31% were senior management (including SVPs and VPs, directors and managers).

More tokens don’t necessarily mean a better outcome. On the contrary, they can cause AI agents to loop, generating large volumes of responses that can run up compute costs and overwhelm a human.

The crux of the issue is translating token consumption into productivity – not equating the two. Token consumption is an input, not an output. It’s the compute era’s equivalent of billable hours: easy to count, weakly correlated with value. Measure outcomes, not token metrics, with the caveat that outcomes are much harder to measure than tokens.

Some metrics that are more useful than tokens to consider include task-completion units (the emerging standard), which count the tasks completed by its agents rather than the tokens processed; cycle-time compression for a given process; and revenue or cost attribution.

AI Adoption and Regulatory Compliance

“Regulatory compliance is slowing us down” has become one of the most common explanations for sluggish AI adoption. The smallest share of survey respondents, 17%, view regulatory compliance as an accelerant for AI adoption.

As government regulations, data privacy laws, and corporate governance requirements increase, the cost to develop, run, and use AI rises significantly. Ensuring that AI acts safely and complies with enterprise parameters requires more “thinking” and therefore more tokens. This is largely because ensuring that models, especially agentic models, are secure, compliant, and safe requires immense computational overhead.

While legal uncertainty and the number of regulations are genuine concerns, large companies also face the buildout of AI bureaucracy, including chief AI officers, adoption dashboards, token budgets or governance councils, according to The Information. This bureaucracy is a mechanism to deploy AI at scale but it also obscures whether any of it pays for itself. The economics of AI, especially in the era of tokenization, can be confusing and the AI bureaucracy itself is not its cause but its symptom.

Common flaws of AI governance include companies governing AI at the policy layer (committees, principles, training) while risk lives at the identity and permission layer. Most policy frameworks are written as instruction sets delivered to the AI model, while the controls that work (deterministic triggers, permission gates, scoped credentials) are enforced outside the model. On top of that, companies may not always know what they are governing, as vendors and employees are adding shadow AI features.

The right approach inverts the framing most companies start with. The default assumption is a tradeoff — compliance slows adoption, so minimize one to maximize the other. The evidence points the other way: the things blocking adoption are the compliance questions, and the companies moving fastest are the ones that resolved them first. But before doing it fast, they must do it right.

Token Cost Management

Token cost management is where the survey’s biggest paradox appears. A slim majority of companies (52%) say they understand token costs, and about as many know that disciplined prompt and output engineering can substantially reduce them. Yet only about a third say they actually control token costs in practice. (See Chart)

“Token cost management is not yet in line with the growth in usage of AI,” one respondent writes.

Only one in five respondents (20%) believe that buying tokens in higher volumes lowers cost-per-query (see Chart). Yet The Information’s research shows that batching purchases is an effective and increasingly necessary strategy for cutting per-query costs on frontier models, which carry a steep premium over simpler ones. Equally important for savings is selecting token-guzzling frontier models only for tasks that require them.

The Information’s research and reader responses point to five ways companies are managing token costs:

  1. Train users. Teach employees about model selection, how to prevent models from overthinking, and how to prompt and structure requests to achieve the most useful output at the lowest token cost. Also, teach employees when not to use AI.
  2. Match the right model to the right task. Route routine queries to cheaper, open-source models and reserve frontier models for genuinely complex reasoning. “If you select the models best aligned with most tasks, token costs are incredibly low. All the news about token costs concerns frontier models, which are rarely required,” one respondent writes.
  3. Optimize prompts. Keep them concise, strip unnecessary context, and reuse outputs where possible. The Information’s research shows that these “token-minimizing” techniques are being deployed to reduce the volume of data a model must process per request.
  4. Cap and track usage. Track token usage against productivity, not just spend, and set daily or weekly caps when usage is outpacing value. At one respondent’s company, employees don’t have unfettered access to tokens: “Only authorized employees may use tokens, following a defined mandate and an allocated development budget based on a cost-benefit analysis.”
  5. Adopt a systemic approach. Some respondents argue that the fix isn’t behavioral at all. “Cost efficiency is largely determined by systemic, deterministic constraints, rather than individuals voluntarily enforcing constraints upon themselves,” one respondent writes. A systemic approach includes creating a single controlled AI gateway (eradicating shadow AI), introducing hard spend ceilings with approval gates, and making the cheapest path automatic.

Looking Ahead

AI is getting more expensive, not less. The shift from chatbots to autonomous agents built for multi-step workflows is the single biggest driver of rising costs, and token-based pricing means uncontrolled usage shows up directly on the bill. Respondents expect that trend to continue: most see AI-related spending rising across the board over the next 12 months. (See Chart)

That’s happening as the enterprise AI market moves past its experimental phase and into one where spending gets scrutinized like any other line item. Companies that haven’t yet built model routing, usage limits, and hard budget caps into their AI programs are likely to keep absorbing costs they can’t fully explain.

Methodology

Based on a survey of 107 senior leaders and professionals, conducted in June and July 2026.

Company size: Forty-five percent of companies surveyed had revenues under $10 million; 20% had revenues of more than $1 billion; 16% had revenues between $10 million and $100 million; 12% had revenues between $100 million and $500 million, and 8% had revenues between $500 million and $1 billion.

Key industry sectors: Thirty-eight percent of companies were from technology, media and telecommunications; 13% from professional services; 10% from healthcare and life sciences; 9% from financial services & capital markets, and the remaining 29% came from the government, retail, public sector and others.

Respondent titles and roles: Forty percent were executive leadership (including CEOs, CIOs and CTOs) and owners; 31% were senior management (including SVPs and VPs, directors and managers).

items.title: HERMES: Contrast-Aware Knowledge Graph Reasoning from Clinical Notes for Patient Outcome Prediction [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: HERMES: Contrast-Aware Knowledge Graph Reasoning from Clinical Notes for Patient Outcome Prediction
items.summary: arXiv:2609.20825v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Clinical predictive models often rely on structured Electronic Health Record data, such as time-series and procedure codes. While recent approaches have begun leveraging unstructured clinical notes, they typically encode them as flat sequences, which may lose explicit relational and temporal structure present in clinical narratives. In response, we propose HERMES, a graph-based framework that operates exclusively on clinical text while preserving clinical relationships. This approach builds on two key ideas. First, personalized Knowledge Graphs (KGs) are constructed through Large-Language-Model-guided extraction from clinical notes with Contrastive Logic Modeling that explicitly captures temporal dynamics and treatment failures and changes in outcomes. Second, a Graph Attention Network synthesizes patient representations through graph-based learning over the KGs. Experiments on MIMIC-III and MIMIC-IV for in-hospital mortality and 30-day readmission prediction show that HERMES consistently outperforms strong text-only baselines. Our findings demonstrate that explicit relational modeling with Contrastive Logic Modeling significantly advances predictive performance.

items.title: TALON: A Temporally Aware Longitudinal Framework for Radiology Report Generation [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: TALON: A Temporally Aware Longitudinal Framework for Radiology Report Generation
items.summary: arXiv:2609.20826v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Current radiology report generation (RRG) models usually produce descriptive reports based on a single examination or only the most recent prior examination, limiting their ability to perform accurate and meaningful longitudinal comparisons and detect subtle interval changes. Although recent approaches have begun to incorporate multiple prior examinations, they usually aggregate a fixed-length history without explicitly modeling the role-dependent relevance of each prior examination before fusion. To address this, we propose TALON, a Temporally Aware LONgitudinal RRG framework that adaptively integrates variable-length patient histories. The underlying Dual-Channel Temporal Fusion Module (DCTFM) compares the current examination with each prior examination through complementary similarity and change channels to capture persistent findings and interval changes, respectively. The specially designed channel-specific attention estimates the relevance of each prior examination, while a learned prior-specific gate adaptively integrates informative longitudinal evidence and suppresses redundancy. Experiments on MIMIC-CXR show that TALON outperforms the current state-of-the-art method on various clinical efficacy and graph-based metrics. When more prior examinations become available, TALON's performance on these metrics improves even further, emphasizing the strength of TALON's DCTFM in modeling longitudinal RRG across longer and more complex patient histories than existing approaches.

items.title: Beyond WER: Entity and Disfluency Recall in Accented Conversational ASR [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Beyond WER: Entity and Disfluency Recall in Accented Conversational ASR
items.summary: arXiv:2609.20828v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: ASR systems optimised for Word Error Rate (WER) often miss named entities and filled pauses in accented conversational English, both critical for language-learning feedback. We present a three-stage pipeline for speakers from India, Indonesia, and Latin America: (1) heuristic SQL filters curating entity-rich training data at 2.8x the entity density of random sampling, (2) regional LoRA adapters fine-tuned on Qwen2.5-Omni-3B producing both verbatim and corrected transcripts in a single forward pass, and (3) a six-category error taxonomy validated by an LLM-based judge (83.8% agreement, 210 human-labelled samples). The pipeline achieves 80-85% entity recall (up from 53-55%), 76-86% filler recall (up from <5%), and 6-10% WER across 6k test utterances, outperforming Whisper and a commercial ASR on entity recall while matching a zero-shot 30B model with 10x fewer parameters. Paired bootstrap tests confirm that curation alone accounts for 2.8-4.2 pp of entity recall gain (p<0.0001).

items.title: Recursive Language Models Generalize Out of Domain [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Recursive Language Models Generalize Out of Domain
items.summary: arXiv:2609.20831v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study when limiting what a language model can see improves learning. We compare standard CoT, the more general learner that reads the full trace, with recursive language models, which restricts itself by solving each subtask in an isolated context. In-distribution, this generality comes for free: CoT can efficiently simulate the recursive rule, so the IID generalization guarantee changes only by a constant factor, and recursion does not offer much. But out of domain, CoT can fit training by relying on context outside the current subtask, i.e. a shortcut that breaks once those tokens change; recursive context isolation rules out this failure mode. Even though CoT's class still covers the recursive rule, simplicity bias picks the shortcut over the truth. Thus, to go beyond distributional accuracy and truly reason, covering the right rule is not enough; this contrasts with classical learning theory.

items.title: PhysioBench: A Unified Benchmark for Physiological Signal Question Answering [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: PhysioBench: A Unified Benchmark for Physiological Signal Question Answering
items.summary: arXiv:2609.20836v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Physiological signals support diverse clinical and monitoring tasks, yet existing physiological signal foundation models typically require task-specific adaptation for each task. Natural language provides a common interface for specifying different prediction objectives, but the ability of current models to follow such instructions across physiological signal modalities remains insufficiently evaluated. To address this gap, we introduce PhysioBench, a unified benchmark for physiological signal question answering. PhysioBench harmonizes annotations from 22 public datasets into 61.4 million questions across 30 tasks. Each question-answer pair is grounded in a signal segment and traceable to its source annotation. We evaluate 21 representative models, including large language models, vision-language models, time-series language models, and physiological signal foundation models under three complementary settings. The results show that none of the evaluated models achieves consistently strong performance across physiological signal modalities and tasks. The incorporation of natural language supports unified prediction across tasks, although performance remains sensitive to question formulation. Beyond these findings, PhysioBench offers an extensible platform for fine-grained analysis and future research on physiological signal understanding. Our codes are available at https://github.com/Leanna97/PhysioBench.

items.title: VISPATH: Visual-Intent-Guided Path Reasoning for Multimodal Knowledge Graph Question Answering [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: VISPATH: Visual-Intent-Guided Path Reasoning for Multimodal Knowledge Graph Question Answering
items.summary: arXiv:2609.20843v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Knowledge graph question answering (KGQA) enables models to answer natural-language questions through structured graph reasoning and has achieved substantial progress across many benchmarks and applications. Recently, multimodal KGQA (MM-KGQA) has attracted increasing attention because many questions require jointly using multimodal inputs and KG evidence. However, existing MM-KGQA methods typically use multimodal information only for starting entity grounding or evidence retrieval, after which multi-hop reasoning degenerates into text-only graph search. As a result, they cannot exploit multimodal cues that become important at intermediate hops. To address this limitation, we propose VISPATH, a visual-intent-guided path reasoning framework for MM-KGQA. VISPATH first identifies a reliable starting entity by combining multimodal grounding with graph-structural cues. It then performs intent-guided path discovery by recomputing hop-specific multimodal intent from the input, question, and current partial paths, so that each expansion is guided by the current reasoning state. The discovered paths are further refined through reasoning-chain pruning, which evaluates candidate paths as complete evidence chains based on their consistency with the question, reasoning sketch, and hop-specific intent. Finally, VISPATH checks whether the selected evidence is sufficient for answer generation. We further construct VISPATH-Bench, a benchmark for evaluating multimodal multi-hop reasoning over KGs, covering questions that require two to four hops over KG paths. Extensive experiments on VISPATH-Bench and three additional multimodal QA benchmarks show that VISPATH consistently outperforms strong baselines. Notably, with GPT-4o as the backbone, VISPATH surpasses GPT-5.4 on VISPATH-Bench, achieving a 10.6% relative improvement in average accuracy and a 13.1% improvement at 2-hop reasoning.
